newsitem.title: DUBAI: Most Gulf businesses family run, short-lived.
newsitem.headline: Most Gulf businesses family run, short-lived.

text.p: Most private businesses in the oil-rich Gulf are family concerns, many of which should float their shares to avoid failure and extend their lives beyond an average 25 years, a leading Gulf businessman said on Monday.

"Only 30 percent of family businesses survive to the second generation. Of this...only 13 percent will go to the third generation," said Khalid Kanoo, group managing director of the Bahrain-based Yusuf Bin Ahmed Kanoo group.
The diversified group, established in 1890, is now run by the sixth generation of Kanoo family members. It has no plans to go public just yet.
"There are only a handful that are 100 years old, most are 10 to 20 years old and the average life is 25 years," he said.
The business scene in the Gulf is dominated by powerful family-owned enterprises that have evolved from small trading houses into multi-million dollar conglomerates.
Analysts say that small investors with limited investment opportunities are crowded out by these large family groups.

Speaking on the sidelines of a conference on family firms, Kanoo said there were 451,621 registered companies in Saudi Arabia in 1996, around 110,000 in Kuwait and 29,000 in Bahrain. In comparison, there are only some 70 listed companies in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait and less than 40 in Bahrain.

"It is so easy for family businesses to die because they are attached to emotional factors not functional ones. When family and business affairs mix, which is the normal case, soon the business disintegrates," he told Reuters.

"Companies that are well run, united and well led do not need to change, but those that are not and anticipate problems should. They can merge or sell the business. But for continuity, going public is the best option in the long term because you have shareholders to answer to," he said.
He said issues of succession, nepotism and sibling rivalry often led to the downfall of family enterprises. Good leadership and a willingness to change would help ensure their survival.
"But resistance is 'how do I sell my baby, which I have looked after since birth', but it should be looked at as 'it will die soon. It has family-business disease'," he said.
Asked if he expected more of these companies to float their shares on the Gulf's developing capital markets, Kanoo said: "Yes. It is catching on and it is no longer a taboo."
